1:5.t: "Grasped": the KJV's "comprehended" can mean either understood or overpowered; the Greek allows both.

1:14.t: "Only Son": the KJV's "only begotten" means the one and only, unique Son.
"Lived among us" (Greek skenoo, "pitch a tent"): the word recalls the tabernacle, the tent where God's glory dwelt among Israel (Exodus 40:34).
"Grace and truth" (Greek charis and aletheia): this likely echoes the Hebrew pair hesed and emet (see Genesis 24:27, Exodus 34:6), God's faithful love and reliability, now seen in Jesus.
"Flesh" (Greek sarx): here sarx means real human nature with its weakness, not sinful nature as in some of Paul's letters (Romans 8). The Word became fully human.

1:18.t: "Only Son": the KJV's "only begotten" means the one and only, unique Son.

1:28.t: Bethabara: the KJV reading; many modern Bibles read "Bethany beyond the Jordan".

1:39.t: "About four in the afternoon": the KJV's "tenth hour", counting from sunrise.

1:42.t: "Son of Jonah": the KJV's "Jona"; many modern Bibles read "son of John".

2:1.t: Cana was a village a few kilometers north of Nazareth.

2:6.t: "About 80 to 120 liters": the KJV's "two or three firkins". The firkin (Greek metretes) held about 40 liters.

2:8.t: "The master of the banquet": the KJV's "the governor of the feast", the guest in charge of the celebration.

2:20.t: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple in about 20 BC; the work went on until AD 64.

3:1.t: "A member of the Jewish ruling council": the KJV's "a ruler of the Jews", a member of the Sanhedrin.

3:13.t: "Who is in heaven": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

3:14.t: "Lifted up" (Greek hypsoo): to raise high and to exalt. In John it means both Jesus' crucifixion and His exaltation (8:28, 12:32-33).

3:15.t: It is not clear where Jesus' words end and John's comment begins; many think Jesus' words end at verse 15. The quotation marks follow that reading.

3:23.t: Aenon ("springs") near Salim was probably in the Jordan Valley.

3:25.t: "The Jews": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "a certain Jew".

4:5.t: Sychar was near Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim. See Genesis 33:18-19 and 48:22.

4:6.t: "About noon": the KJV's "about the sixth hour".

4:9.t: Jews regarded Samaritans as a mixed people with a corrupted worship, and avoided using the same vessels.

4:20.t: "This mountain": Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans had built a temple.

4:35.t: "Four months more and then the harvest": perhaps a proverb about waiting.

4:46.t: "A royal official": the KJV's "a certain nobleman", probably an officer of Herod Antipas.

4:52.t: "One in the afternoon": the KJV's "the seventh hour".

5:2.t: "Near the Sheep Gate": the KJV's "by the sheep market"; the Greek has only "by the sheep", so a word must be supplied. "Aramaic": the KJV's "the Hebrew tongue". "Bethesda": the KJV's reading; some manuscripts read "Bethzatha". Excavations have found a pool with five porticoes.

5:3.t: "Waiting for the moving of the water ... whatever disease they had": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

5:29.t: "To be condemned": the KJV's "unto the resurrection of damnation". See Matthew 23:33.

6:1.t: The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee, named after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore in honor of the emperor Tiberius.

6:7.t: "Two hundred denarii": the KJV's "two hundred pennyworth", about eight months' wages.

6:19.t: "About five or six kilometers": the KJV's "about five and twenty or thirty furlongs".

6:31.t: A quotation of Exodus 16:4 and Psalm 78:24.

6:47.t: "In Me": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

6:69.t: "The Christ, the Son of the living God": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the Holy One of God".

6:71.t: "Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "Judas son of Simon Iscariot".

7:2.t: The Festival of Tabernacles (Booths) in the autumn remembered Israel's years in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:33-43).

7:8.t: "Not yet going up": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "not going up".

7:37.t: Each day of the festival, priests poured water from the pool of Siloam at the altar. The Scripture Jesus refers to may be Isaiah 58:11, Ezekiel 47:1-12 or Zechariah 14:8. "From within them": the KJV's "out of his belly", the inner self.

7:39.t: "The Spirit had not been given": the KJV's "the Holy Ghost was not yet given". The Greek says literally "the Spirit was not yet".

7:53.t: The KJV includes this passage. The earliest manuscripts do not have it, and some later ones place it elsewhere in John or in Luke. Many think it is a true story from early tradition that was added later.

8:5.t: See Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22-24, which required both the man and the woman to be put to death.

8:20.t: "Near the place where the offerings were put": the KJV's "in the treasury".

9:7.t: The Pool of Siloam was at the south end of Jerusalem, fed by Hezekiah's tunnel (2 Kings 20:20).

9:22.t: Being put out of the synagogue meant being cut off from the Jewish community.

9:24.t: "Give glory to God": a solemn charge to tell the truth (Joshua 7:19).

10:16.t: "One fold": the KJV's reading. The Greek has two different words: aule, "sheep pen", earlier in the verse, and poimne, "flock", here. Many modern Bibles read "one flock".

10:22.t: The Festival of Dedication (Hanukkah) in December celebrated the rededication of the temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC, after Antiochus IV had defiled it.

10:23.t: Solomon's Colonnade was a covered walkway along the east side of the temple courts.

10:34.t: A quotation of Psalm 82:6, where "gods" refers to human judges.

11:16.t: "Didymus": Greek for "twin", as "Thomas" is in Aramaic.

11:18.t: "Less than three kilometers": the KJV's "about fifteen furlongs".

11:44.t: "A cloth": the KJV's "a napkin", a cloth wrapped around the face of the dead.

11:48.t: "Our temple": the KJV's "our place", meaning the temple.

11:54.t: Ephraim was a village about 20 kilometers north of Jerusalem.

12:3.t: "About 330 grams": the KJV's "a pound"; Greek litra, the Roman pound. "Pure nard": the KJV's "spikenard". See Mark 14:3.

12:5.t: "Three hundred denarii": the KJV's "three hundred pence", about a year's wages.

12:13.t: Palm branches were a symbol of Jewish national hope. The words come from Psalm 118:25-26.

12:41.t: "His glory": the KJV's reading; Isaiah saw the glory of the Lord (Isaiah 6:1-5), and John says it was Christ's glory.

13:4.t: "Outer clothing": the KJV's "garments". Washing feet was the work of the lowest servant.

13:18.t: A quotation of Psalm 41:9. "Turned against Me": the KJV's "hath lifted up his heel against me", an image of betrayal.

13:23.t: "Reclining next to Him": the KJV's "leaning on Jesus' bosom". Guests lay on their left side at the table, so the one on Jesus' right lay close to His chest. "The disciple whom Jesus loved" is traditionally identified as John, the writer of this Gospel (21:20-24).

13:26.t: "Piece of bread": the KJV's "sop". Offering a choice morsel was a mark of honor.

14:2.t: "Dwelling places": the KJV's "mansions", which in 1611 meant places to stay or rooms, not large houses. The Greek mone is from meno, "to remain" (see 6:56; also 14:23, "home").

14:22.t: Judas (not Iscariot) is probably Judas the son of James (Luke 6:16), also called Thaddaeus.

15:1.t: "Gardener": the KJV's "husbandman", the farmer who tends the vine.

15:25.t: A quotation of Psalm 35:19 and 69:4. "Their Law" here means the Scriptures in general.

16:2.t: "Offering a service to God": the KJV's "doeth God service", offering worship.

17:12.t: "The son of destruction": the KJV's "the son of perdition", Judas. The phrase is a Hebrew idiom for one destined for destruction (compare 2 Thessalonians 2:3). The Scripture is probably Psalm 41:9 (see 13:18).

17:15.t: "From evil": the KJV's "from the evil"; the Greek can mean "from evil" or "from the evil one".

18:1.t: "The Kidron Valley": the KJV's "the brook Cedron", a ravine between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, dry except in the rainy season.

18:3.t: "A detachment of soldiers": the KJV's "a band", a Roman cohort, or part of one.

18:13.t: On Annas and Caiaphas, see Luke 3:2.

18:28.t: "The palace of the Roman governor": the KJV's "the hall of judgment", the Praetorium. Entering a Gentile house would make a Jew ceremonially unclean.

18:31.t: Under Roman rule, the Jewish council could not carry out a death sentence. Jesus had said He would be "lifted up" (12:32-33), which meant crucifixion, a Roman punishment, not stoning.

19:13.t: "Aramaic": the KJV's "Hebrew", meaning the language spoken by the Jews at the time. Also 19:17 and 19:20; in 19:20 the KJV's "Hebrew" is kept.

19:14.t: "About noon": the KJV's "about the sixth hour". Mark 15:25 says Jesus was crucified at "the third hour"; John may count hours differently, or round them.

19:29.t: Hyssop is a small plant used in the Passover ritual (Exodus 12:22).

19:31.t: Breaking the legs hastened death, since the crucified could no longer push up to breathe.

19:36.t: A quotation of Exodus 12:46, Numbers 9:12 and Psalm 34:20. Not one bone of the Passover lamb was to be broken.

19:39.t: "About 33 kilograms": the KJV's "about an hundred pound weight", a hundred Roman pounds, a burial fit for a king.

20:16.t: "Rabboni": Aramaic, "my teacher", a warm and respectful form of "Rabbi". "Aramaic": the KJV has no language named here; many manuscripts add "in Hebrew".

21:7.t: "He had taken it off": the KJV's "for he was naked", meaning stripped for work, wearing only an undergarment.

21:8.t: "About ninety meters": the KJV's "as it were two hundred cubits".

21:15.t: "Simon son of Jonah": the KJV's "Simon, son of Jonas"; many early manuscripts read "Simon son of John".

"Love": Jesus' first two questions use agapao; Peter answers each time with phileo, warm personal love. The third time Jesus uses phileo, and Peter is grieved. Some see a deliberate contrast: Peter, humbled by his denial, will not claim the higher love. Others note that John uses the two words interchangeably (compare 3:35 and 5:20) and that the point is the threefold question matching Peter's threefold denial (18:17, 25, 27). This translation uses "love" for both and records the difference here. "Feed ... take care of" (Greek bosko ... poimaino): to feed, and to shepherd. Jesus restores Peter and gives him the charge of His flock.

21:25.t: "Amen": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have it.

1:1.t: "The Word" (Greek logos): logos means word, message, or the reason behind something. To Jewish readers it called to mind God creating by His word (Genesis 1:3, Psalm 33:6). To Greek readers it meant the reason that orders the universe. John uses both ideas and then says something new: the Logos is a person who was with God and was God.

"The Word was God" (Greek theos en ho logos): "God" comes first for emphasis and has no article. This tells us the Word shares God's nature, while "the Word was with God" keeps the Word distinct from the Father. It does not mean "a god", a reading the grammar does not require and the rest of John rules out (1:18, 20:28).

1:17.t: "Grace and truth" (Greek charis and aletheia): this likely echoes the Hebrew pair hesed and emet (see Genesis 24:27, Exodus 34:6), God's faithful love and reliability, now seen in Jesus.

2:4.t: "Woman" (Greek gynai): a respectful form of address, not harsh (Jesus uses it from the cross, 19:26). "Why do you involve Me?": literally "what to Me and to you?", a Hebrew idiom meaning "this is not our concern" or "leave this to Me". "My hour": in John, the hour of Jesus' death and glorification (12:23, 13:1, 17:1).

2:11.t: "Signs" (Greek semeion): John calls Jesus' miracles signs, because they point beyond themselves to who He is. The book is built around seven of them.

2:19.t: "Temple" (Greek naos): the sanctuary itself. Jesus' body is the true dwelling of God among people (1:14).

3:3.t: "Born again" (Greek gennethe anothen): anothen means both "again" and "from above". Nicodemus hears "again"; Jesus means a new birth from God (1:13).

3:5.t: "Born of water and the Spirit": readers understand this as natural birth and spiritual birth, as baptism and the Spirit, or as the cleansing and renewing of the Spirit promised in Ezekiel 36:25-27, which Nicodemus as "Israel's teacher" should have known (3:10).

3:8.t: "Wind ... Spirit" (Greek pneuma): one word means both wind and spirit, like the Hebrew ruach. Jesus plays on it: the Spirit is like the wind, unseen but known by its effects.

3:16.t: "Loved" (Greek egapesen, from agapao): see Matthew 5:43-44. God's love is shown in giving. "Only Son" (Greek monogenes): the KJV's "only begotten"; see 1:14. "Eternal life" (Greek zoe aionios): the KJV's "everlasting life", the life of the age to come, which begins now for those who believe (5:24, 17:3).

3:36.t: "Wrath" (Greek orge): God's settled opposition to sin. John uses the word only here.

4:10.t: "Living water" (Greek hydor zon): in ordinary speech, fresh running water from a spring. Jesus means the life God gives through the Spirit (7:37-39). Compare Jeremiah 2:13.

4:23.t: "In the Spirit and in truth": the KJV's "in spirit and in truth". The Greek has no capital letters; many take "spirit" as the Holy Spirit, others as the human spirit. "God is spirit" (Greek pneuma ho theos): the KJV's "God is a Spirit". He is not bound to any place, so true worship is not tied to one mountain or temple.

4:26.t: "I ... am He" (Greek ego eimi): literally "I am". See Matthew 14:27. This is the first of many "I am" sayings in John.

5:17.t: "My Father is always at His work": God continues to sustain the world on the Sabbath. By claiming the same right, Jesus claims equality with God, as His hearers understood.

5:24.t: "Judged" (Greek krisis): judgment or condemnation. The believer has already passed from death to life.

5:39.t: "Search the Scriptures": the KJV's reading, taking the verb as a command. The Greek eraunate can also be a statement, "You search the Scriptures".

6:14.t: "The Prophet": the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15-18 (compare 1:21, 7:40).

6:35.t: "I am the bread of life": the first of seven "I am" sayings in John with a picture attached (also 8:12, 10:7, 10:11, 11:25, 14:6, 15:1). On ego eimi, see 4:26.

6:44.t: "Draws" (Greek helkyo): to pull or drag, used of hauling a net (21:6). No one comes to Christ by their own power; the Father draws them. Jesus uses the same word in 12:32: "I will draw all people to Myself."

6:51.t: "Eat My flesh ... drink My blood": Jesus speaks of giving His body in death "for the life of the world". Christians differ on how far these words point to the Lord's Supper; all agree they call for receiving Christ Himself by faith (6:35, 6:47).

6:56.t: "Remains" (Greek meno): the KJV's "dwelleth", to abide or stay. A key word in John (15:4-10, 1 John 2:24-28) for a lasting union with Christ.

6:63.t: "The Spirit gives life; the flesh counts for nothing": "flesh" (sarx) here means human nature on its own, without God's Spirit (compare 3:6). Jesus' words are to be understood spiritually, not crudely.

8:12.t: "I am the light of the world": during the Festival of Tabernacles great lamps were lit in the temple court. Light also recalls the pillar of fire in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21).

8:24.t: "I am He" (Greek ego eimi): literally "I am". See 4:26 and 8:58.

8:28.t: "I am He" (Greek ego eimi): literally "I am". See 4:26 and 8:58.

8:32.t: "Truth" (Greek aletheia): in John, not just correct facts but God's reality revealed in Jesus (1:14, 14:6). Knowing it frees people from slavery to sin (8:34).

8:58.t: "Before Abraham was born, I am!" (Greek prin Abraam genesthai ego eimi): Jesus does not say "I was" but "I am", the name God gave Himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). His hearers understood it as a claim to be God and tried to stone Him for blasphemy (8:59, compare 10:33).

9:3.t: Jesus rejects the idea that every suffering is punishment for a particular sin (compare Luke 13:1-5). God's work will be shown in the man.

9:39.t: "Blind ... see": physical sight becomes a picture of spiritual sight. Those who admit their blindness receive sight; those who claim to see remain in their sin.

10:11.t: "The good shepherd" (Greek ho poimen ho kalos): kalos means good, noble, beautiful. God is Israel's shepherd (Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34:11-16); Jesus takes the role. "Lays down His life" (Greek psyche): see Matthew 16:25-26.

10:28.t: "No one will snatch them out of My hand ... out of My Father's hand": the security of believers rests on the hands of the Son and the Father together.

10:30.t: "I and the Father are one" (Greek hen esmen): "one" is neuter, "one thing", not "one person". It means one in nature and purpose, while Father and Son remain distinct (compare 17:21-22). His hearers took it as a claim to be God (10:33).

11:3.t: "Love": two Greek words are used. In 11:3 and 11:36 it is phileo, warm personal affection; in 11:5 it is agapao, committed love. John uses them closely together; see 21:15-17.

11:5.t: "Love": two Greek words are used. In 11:3 and 11:36 it is phileo, warm personal affection; in 11:5 it is agapao, committed love. John uses them closely together; see 21:15-17.

11:36.t: "Love": two Greek words are used. In 11:3 and 11:36 it is phileo, warm personal affection; in 11:5 it is agapao, committed love. John uses them closely together; see 21:15-17.

11:25.t: "I am the resurrection and the life": the fifth "I am" saying (see 6:35). Jesus does not merely promise resurrection at the last day (11:24); He is its source now.

11:33.t: "Deeply moved" (Greek embrimaomai): a strong word that can mean to snort with anger or indignation. Jesus is moved by grief and by anger at death itself.

11:38.t: "Deeply moved" (Greek embrimaomai): a strong word that can mean to snort with anger or indignation. Jesus is moved by grief and by anger at death itself.

11:35.t: "Jesus wept" (Greek edakrysen): He shed tears quietly, unlike the loud wailing of the mourners (Greek klaio, 11:33). The shortest verse in the KJV shows His full humanity.

11:50.t: Caiaphas meant it as political expediency; John sees in his words an unintended prophecy of Jesus' death "for" (Greek hyper, on behalf of) the people.

12:23.t: "The hour has come": see 2:4. The coming of the Greeks signals that the time for Jesus' death and glory has arrived.

12:31.t: "The prince of this world": Satan (14:30, 16:11). The cross is his defeat.

12:32.t: "Lifted up": see 3:14. "Draw" (Greek helkyo): see 6:44. "All people": the KJV's "all men"; Jews and Gentiles alike.

13:1.t: "To the end" (Greek eis telos): to the uttermost, and to the end of His life. Compare 19:30, "It is finished" (tetelestai).

13:8.t: "Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me": the foot washing pictures the cleansing Jesus gives by His death. Without it no one belongs to Him.

13:34.t: "A new command": the command to love was old (Leviticus 19:18); the new standard is "as I have loved you". "Love" here and through John 13-17 is agapao and agape. See Matthew 5:43-44.

14:6.t: "I am the way and the truth and the life": the sixth "I am" saying (see 6:35). Jesus does not only show the way; He is the way to the Father.

14:16.t: "Advocate" (Greek parakletos): the KJV's "Comforter". The word means one called alongside to help: a counselor, advocate, helper, or comforter. No single English word covers it. "Another" (Greek allos) means another of the same kind: the Spirit continues Jesus' own presence. 1 John 2:1 uses the same word of Jesus.

14:26.t: "Advocate" (Greek parakletos): the KJV's "Comforter". The word means one called alongside to help: a counselor, advocate, helper, or comforter. No single English word covers it. "Another" (Greek allos) means another of the same kind: the Spirit continues Jesus' own presence. 1 John 2:1 uses the same word of Jesus.

14:27.t: "Peace" (Greek eirene, Hebrew shalom): see Luke 2:14. Jesus' farewell gift.

14:28.t: "The Father is greater than I": spoken by the Son who had taken on human nature and was going to the Father. Christians have understood it of His role as the one sent, not as a denial of the oneness He claimed (10:30, 14:9).

15:2.t: "Cuts off ... prunes" (Greek airei ... kathairei): a wordplay. Kathairei, "prunes", also means "cleanses", linking to 15:3, "you are already clean" (katharoi).

15:4.t: "Remain" (Greek meno): the KJV's "abide". See 6:56. The word occurs ten times in these verses.

15:13.t: "Friends" (Greek philoi, from phileo): those loved with warm, personal affection. Jesus raises His disciples from servants to friends.

15:26.t: "Goes out from the Father" (Greek para tou patros ekporeuetai): the KJV's "proceedeth from the Father". This verse lies behind the words of the Nicene Creed about the Holy Spirit. Western and Eastern churches have long differed over whether the Spirit proceeds "from the Father and the Son".

16:8.t: "Prove the world to be in the wrong" (Greek elencho): the KJV's "reprove". To expose, convict, bring to light. The Spirit acts as prosecutor, showing the world its guilt.

16:33.t: "Trouble" (Greek thlipsis): the KJV's "tribulation", pressure, distress. "Overcome" (Greek nikao): to conquer, to win the victory, a key word in 1 John and Revelation.

17:3.t: "Know" (Greek ginosko): see Matthew 7:23. Eternal life is a living relationship with God.

17:17.t: "Sanctify" (Greek hagiazo): to make holy, set apart for God. Jesus sets Himself apart (17:19) for His sacrificial death so that His people may be set apart for God.

17:21.t: "One": see 10:30. The unity of believers is to mirror the unity of Father and Son.

18:5.t: "I am He" (Greek ego eimi): see 4:26 and 8:58. At the words "I am", the arresting party drew back and fell to the ground.

18:8.t: "I am He" (Greek ego eimi): see 4:26 and 8:58. At the words "I am", the arresting party drew back and fell to the ground.

18:36.t: "My kingdom is not of this world" (Greek ouk estin ek tou kosmou toutou): its source and authority are not from this world; it does not mean His kingdom has nothing to do with the world.

19:5.t: "Here is the man!" (Latin Ecce homo): Pilate presents Jesus mockingly, but John's readers see the true man, the Son of Man.

19:30.t: "It is finished" (Greek tetelestai): one word meaning "it is accomplished, completed, paid in full". Jesus has finished the work the Father gave Him (17:4). "Gave up His spirit" (Greek paredoken to pneuma): He handed over His spirit, a deliberate act (10:18).

19:34.t: "Blood and water": a sign of real death, witnessed and solemnly affirmed. Christians have also seen in it pictures of cleansing and life (7:38-39, 1 John 5:6-8).

20:17.t: "Do not hold on to Me" (Greek me mou haptou): the KJV's "Touch me not". The present tense means "stop clinging to Me". Mary need not hold Him; He is going to the Father, and a new relationship will begin.

20:22.t: "He breathed on them" (Greek enephysesen): the same verb used when God breathed life into Adam (Genesis 2:7, Greek). Jesus gives His disciples the breath of new life, the Spirit.

20:23.t: "If you forgive anyone's sins": the KJV's "whose soever sins ye remit". Christians differ on how the church exercises this authority: through proclaiming the gospel, through church discipline, or through a ministry of absolution. Compare Matthew 16:19 and 18:18.

20:28.t: "My Lord and my God!" (Greek ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou): the climax of John's Gospel, which began, "the Word was God" (1:1). Jesus accepts the confession.

20:31.t: "These are written that you may believe": John's own statement of why he wrote. "Believe" (Greek pisteuo): see Mark 1:15. Some manuscripts read "continue to believe".

21:18.t: "Stretch out your hands": early Christian tradition records that Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, about AD 64.
